Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-prompt-long-0030", "row_sha256": "5e21bdae713ffbc31b8e52bfe0836c8a877f245da405e3ad51b5eb2dc41f9bc1", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hi, can you turn these notes into one self-contained update for our family meal calendar for the week of october 14–20. it should sound like an ordinary family update, not a formal plan or a recipe collection. the people involved are Mara and Luis and their kids Ana, who is 12, and Ben, who is 8. Mara usually updates the paper calendar on the fridge after the Sunday grocery run, and Luis also has a phone copy. This update is for them, not for a public audience, so don't explain what a family meal calendar is. Keep it focused on this one week, and don't turn it into a general system for planning future meals.

some of these notes are already in the calendar and some are not settled yet, which matters. the entries use green for confirmed, yellow for tentative, and a blank space when nobody has chosen dinner. Thursday tacos are green. Sunday baked potatoes are green if the grocery pickup happens as planned. Tuesday lentil soup is yellow, not confirmed. Wednesday and Saturday are blank. Monday might be leftovers from the roast they had on the previous Sunday, but only if there is enough left; it should not sound like that is definite. Friday has frozen dumplings listed, but nobody has said whether they are actually eating those, so that's not a confirmed dinner either. Please make the difference between confirmed, tentative, conditional, and undecided clear. Don't quietly fill in blank days just to make the week look complete.

There are details about the week that help explain the entries, and i want them used without stretching them. Mara has a late clinic shift on Tuesday, so the soup depends on whether she gets home in time to have dinner with everyone. Luis said, “If the soup is on Tuesday, I can pick up the bread after work.” keep his actual words as a normal quote if you use them, and don't make it sound like he has already bought bread. Ana's choir ends at 6:30 on Wednesday. That explains why a quick dinner might be useful, but nobody has picked a Wednesday meal, so don't decide one for them. Luis is the one who usually cooks on Thursdays, and he has confirmed that he will make tacos this Thursday. That is the firmest dinner entry. For the tacos, the shopping note says tortillas, beans, and salsa; don't add a menu of toppings or claim anyone has a preference that isn't in these notes.

The shopping details are on a separate scrap of paper, so please make them easy to spot in the update, but don't turn them into a complete shopping list for meals that aren't settled. For Tuesday soup the scrap lists lentils, carrots, and onions. The tortillas, beans, and salsa are for Thursday. The Sunday baked potatoes depend on the grocery pickup: Mara has put potatoes on the list but hasn't confirmed the pickup yet. The family already has frozen dumplings, which is why they appear on Friday's calendar, but that fact by itself does not mean Friday's plan is confirmed. There is no grocery note for the open Wednesday or Saturday entries. Don't imply the family has ingredients for an unchosen meal on either of those days.

One practical detail: the fridge calendar and Luis's phone copy should match after Mara makes the Sunday update. He sometimes checks the phone copy when he is on the way home, so the wording should make it easy to see which entries have changed status and what still needs a decision. Don't say that either copy has already been updated; this is the update text they are preparing. There is no need to describe a reminder or propose who should decide the blank entries. Keep names and ages as given, and don't add dietary requirements, allergies, school schedules beyond Ana's choir, extra relatives, or other reasons for the meals.

Please organize the update with a short opening that names the week and the household, then a numbered section that groups the calendar entries in a sensible way. It can distinguish the confirmed meals from the not-yet-set ones, as long as the day and status remain clear. Include the shopping notes near the relevant entries or in a small separate part so they are not confused with confirmed dinner plans. The quote can sit beside Tuesday's entry. Use connected, natural paragraphs rather than a bare list of ingredients, and don't repeat the same status explanation in every paragraph. This is an update, not a finished menu: keep the uncertain details uncertain and don't supply recipes or substitute dishes.

At the end, include a distinct final paragraph with the assessment of the current week: the calendar is useful as a shopping guide for the meals already named, but it is not a complete week plan because Wednesday and Saturday have no dinner entry and Monday depends on whether Sunday's roast leaves enough leftovers. Keep that assessment limited to the October 14–20 week and don't call the schedule finalized. Don't add a concluding summary or recommendation after that paragraph. Make the whole update self-contained, with enough context that someone reading either copy can tell what is firm, what depends on another event, and what remains open.", "output": "Write one self-contained, ordinary family update for the meal calendar for October 14–20. The update is for Mara and Luis and their children, Ana (12) and Ben (8). Keep it focused on this week; do not explain what a family meal calendar is or turn the update into a general meal-planning system. Mara usually updates the paper calendar on the fridge after the Sunday grocery run, and Luis also has a phone copy. Do not say the copies have already been updated; this is the text they are preparing so the two copies can match.

Use natural, connected paragraphs and a short opening that names the week and household. Follow it with a numbered section that makes the calendar entries easy to scan. Keep each day and its status clear, distinguishing confirmed, tentative, conditional, and undecided plans. This is an update, not a finished menu: do not fill blank days, supply recipes or substitute dishes, or make uncertain details sound settled.

1. **Calendar entries and context**

- **Monday:** Leftovers from the roast the family had the previous Sunday are possible only if enough remains. Keep this conditional, not confirmed.
- **Tuesday:** Lentil soup is tentative, not confirmed. Mara has a late clinic shift, and the plan depends on whether she gets home in time to have dinner with everyone. Luis said, “If the soup is on Tuesday, I can pick up the bread after work.” Keep his words as a normal quote if included; do not imply that he has already bought the bread.
- **Wednesday:** No dinner has been chosen, so this entry remains blank. Ana’s choir ends at 6:30. That may explain why a quick dinner would be useful, but do not choose one for the family.
- **Thursday:** Tacos are confirmed. Luis has confirmed that he will cook. The shopping note for this meal is tortillas, beans, and salsa. Do not add toppings or claim that anyone has a preference not given here.
- **Friday:** Frozen dumplings are listed on the calendar, but nobody has confirmed whether they will eat them. Make clear that the listing does not establish a confirmed dinner.
- **Saturday:** No dinner has been chosen; leave the entry open.
- **Sunday:** Baked potatoes are confirmed only if the grocery pickup happens as planned. Mara has put potatoes on the grocery list but has not confirmed the pickup, so preserve the condition.

2. **Shopping notes**

Make the notes easy to find, either beside the relevant calendar entries or in a small separate part of the update. The Tuesday soup note lists lentils, carrots, and onions. The Thursday taco note lists tortillas, beans, and salsa. The Sunday note lists potatoes, with the baked-potato dinner dependent on the grocery pickup. The family already has frozen dumplings, which explains their appearance on Friday’s calendar but does not confirm that meal. There is no grocery note for Wednesday or Saturday, and no chosen meal for either day. Do not present these notes as a complete shopping list for unsettled dinners.

Keep the update practical for Luis, who sometimes checks the phone copy on his way home, so it is easy to see what is confirmed, what has changed status, and what still needs a decision. Do not propose who should decide the open entries. Do not add dietary requirements, allergies, relatives, school schedules beyond Ana’s choir, or other reasons for the meals. Preserve the names and ages as given.

End with a distinct final paragraph assessing only this week: the calendar is useful as a shopping guide for the meals already named, but it is not a complete week plan because Wednesday and Saturday have no dinner entry and Monday depends on whether Sunday’s roast leaves enough leftovers. Keep the assessment limited to October 14–20 and do not call the schedule finalized. Do not add a concluding summary or recommendation after that paragraph. The finished update should be self-contained and make clear what is firm, what depends on another event, and what remains open."}]
